newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt to unveil planned tax cuts at 1100 GMT.
newsitem.headline: German govt to unveil planned tax cuts at 1100 GMT.

text.p: Germany's coalition government, which has been wrangling for months over plans to overhaul the country's tax system, was due on Thursday to publish two key tax cuts to take effect in 1998.

Leaders from the three parties in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's alliance were due to announce at 1100 GMT a two-point cut in an unpopular 7.5 percent income tax surcharge raised to help rebuild east Germany, taking effect on January 1, 1998.

At talks on Wednesday the coalition agreed that corporation taxes should also be cut in 1998. The rate on retained profits will fall from 45 to 35 percent and that on profits distributed to shareholder from 30 to 25 percent, coalition sources said.

The sources said the 35 percent rate on retained profits should be in line with a lower top rate of income tax to come in under the main tax reform in 1999, but no final decision has been reached on this. The top rate now is 53 percent.
To finance the corporation tax cuts, which are intended to stimulate the economy, opportunities for writeoffs and to channel funds into reserves would be restricted.

The cuts in the so-called solidarity surcharge, worth eight billion marks, and in corporation taxes are a breakthrough for the Free Democrats (FDP), the junior coalition party which has staked its political survival on forcing through reductions.

But the overall outline of the tax reform remains vague, with a coalition policy commission chaired by Finance Minister Theo Waigel now running behind schedule and only expected to wrap up its work in late January.
